core: The working definition of working capital: the money a business uses to run its day-to-day operations, equal to current assets minus current liabilities — attributed to CFI

The four components named — cash, accounts receivable, inventory, and accounts payable — each with one line and an original example; the accounts themselves are owned by the accounting subject and referenced only
The working capital cycle — buy, sell, collect — with an original example
Why it matters: a business can be profitable and still choke on day-to-day cash; cash flow is the sibling topic that owns the flow story
Managing working capital: speeding collections, watching inventory, and timing payments, each named generally
Too much versus too little: idle cash versus missed payments — the trade-off, stated simply
The honest framing: working capital is the business's day-to-day oxygen
outOfScope: Cash flow analysis, inflows and outflows over a period, and cash-flow statements (own sibling topic: finance:foundations:cash-flow)
Corporate finance: capital structure, cost of capital, and long-term financing (own sibling topic: finance:foundations:corporate-finance)
The accounts-receivable, accounts-payable, and inventory accounts themselves, their journal entries, and their reporting (owned by the accounting subject)
Financial ratios such as the current ratio and their formulas (owned by the accounting subject; finance view in finance:foundations:financial-ratios)

claims.claim: Working capital is the money a business uses to fund its day-to-day operations; the working definition used in this lesson is current assets minus current liabilities.
Current assets are cash plus other assets expected to be converted to cash within about a year, with accounts receivable and inventory among the leading examples.
Current liabilities are obligations expected to be settled within one year or less, with accounts payable as the leading example.
The working capital cycle runs buy, sell, collect: a business buys materials on credit, sells its inventory, and then receives payment from customers, at which point the cycle is complete.
Businesses typically manage the working capital cycle by selling inventory quickly, collecting revenue from customers quickly, and paying bills slowly to optimize cash flow.
The financial manager's goal is to manage current assets so the firm has enough cash to pay its bills as they come due and to support its accounts receivable and inventory.
Excess inventory reduces the amount of working capital a company has on hand and can force the company to borrow money to cover it.
Cash held in low-interest accounts earns little if any interest, so financial managers keep cash balances lean and invest surplus cash in short-term securities.
Negative working capital can be a sign of efficiency in businesses with low inventory and accounts receivable, or a warning sign that a company lacks enough cash to pay its current liabilities.
Fast-growing companies can run themselves out of money — CFI's warning is not to 'grow the company out of money' — which is why working capital matters even for businesses that look successful.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is negative working capital good or bad?
positions: CFI notes that negative working capital can be a sign of efficiency in businesses with low inventory and accounts receivable, such as grocery retail, where customers pay upfront and suppliers extend credit.
CFI also notes that negative working capital may signal financial trouble when a company does not have enough cash to pay its current liabilities.
This lesson holds both honestly: the sign is not the story — the business's ability to pay its bills on time is.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How much working capital is the right amount?
positions: OpenStax's Introduction to Business notes that cash in low-interest accounts earns little, so financial managers keep cash balances low and invest surpluses.
The same source stresses that cash is the lifeblood of business and that the financial manager's goal is to keep enough cash to pay bills as they come due.
This lesson states the trade-off simply: too little means missed payments, too much means idle cash — the right pool is the smallest one that keeps the bills paid on time.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Where is the line between working capital and cash flow?
positions: Working capital is a stock: the pool of cash and near-cash available for day-to-day operations at a point in time.
Cash flow is a flow: money moving into and out of the business over a period.
This lesson keeps them separate and names cash flow as the sibling topic (finance:foundations:cash-flow) that owns the movement over time; here working capital is the pool the daily loop draws from.

sourceRecords.title: Working Capital Cycle
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Reused from the phase-2 source registry (id cfi-working-capital-cycle); re-verified live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. Supports: the working definition of working capital as current assets less current liabilities; the working capital cycle as buy materials on credit, sell inventory, collect payment from customers; managing the cycle by selling inventory quickly, collecting revenue quickly, and paying bills slowly; negative working capital as efficiency in low-inventory businesses or a distress signal when current liabilities cannot be paid; and the growth warning not to 'grow the company out of money.' Facts synthesized into original prose; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Introduction to Business, Section 16.2: How Organizations Use Funds
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (open textbook). Read on 2026-08-21 via an Internet Archive capture (2021-08-05, server-rendered page) of the canonical section URL, since openstax.org serves a JavaScript shell to curl. Supports: short-term expenses resulting in current assets, which include cash and any other assets (accounts receivable and inventory) convertible to cash within a year; the financial manager managing current assets so the firm has enough cash to pay its bills; cash as the lifeblood of business; the three cash-management strategies of collecting money owed as quickly as possible, paying money owed as late as possible without damaging credit reputation, and minimizing funds tied up in inventory; excess inventory reducing working capital on hand and forcing borrowing; and low-interest checking accounts motivating lean cash balances with surplus invested in marketable securities. Facts synthesized into original prose; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Accounting, Volume 1: Financial Accounting, Section 2.2: Define, Explain, and Provide Examples of Current and Noncurrent Assets, Current and Noncurrent Liabilities, Equity, Revenues, and Expenses
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (open textbook). Reused from the phase-2 source registry (registered by the accounting subject); re-verified on 2026-08-21 via an Internet Archive capture of the canonical section URL. Supports the current-versus-noncurrent framing used in this lesson: assets expected to be converted to cash, sold, or used up within one year classified as current assets (accounts receivable as outstanding customer debt on a credit sale; inventory as the value of products to be sold); liabilities expected to be settled within one year classified as current liabilities (accounts payable as the value of goods or services purchased to be paid later). Used here only to name and frame the components; the accounts themselves belong to the accounting subject. Facts synthesized into original prose; no wording reproduced.
